items.sentence: Don't conflate algorithmic trading with AI trading: many algorithms follow simple rules.

items.definition: used to introduce a question that has not been answered yet

items.definition: very different from, and usually much less than

items.sentence: One shared model could become the system's Achilles' heel.

items.sentence: The IMF judges that the risks currently appear contained; the FSB warns that common models could increase correlations in trading; Gensler and Bailey hypothesise that broad adoption could produce a monoculture.
items.definition: Choose the reporting verb to match how firm the source is: judge, warn, hypothesise, argue, concede.

items.sentence: On our reading, it is only when people can declare and answer that a group becomes a society.
items.definition: 'It is only when X that Y' stresses that Y depends on X. More emphatic than 'Y happens only when X'.

items.sentence: Were every firm to rely on one model, their errors would tend to coincide.
items.definition: A formal way to state an unlikely condition: 'Were X to do Y, …' instead of 'If X did Y, …'.

items.sentence: Rarely does a single toy settle a question about real markets.
items.definition: After 'rarely', 'seldom' or 'little' at the start of a clause, put the auxiliary before the subject. Formal writing and talks.

items.sentence: The IMF's finding that a human trader may ultimately make the trading decision implies that deciding is still largely human; from it we infer that full automation is not imminent.
items.wrong: From the IMF's finding we imply that deciding is still largely human.
items.right: From the IMF's finding we infer that deciding is still largely human.
items.definition: Evidence or a speaker implies (suggests); a reader or listener infers (concludes).

items.sentence: Knowledge is one criterion for successful delegation; an incentive is the other.
items.wrong: Knowledge is one criteria for successful delegation.
items.right: Knowledge is one criterion for successful delegation; an incentive is the other.
items.definition: 'Criterion' is singular and 'criteria' plural (likewise phenomenon/phenomena).

items.sentence: Automating the checker raises the question of who checks the checker.
items.wrong: Automating the checker begs the question of who checks the checker.
items.right: Automating the checker raises the question of who checks the checker.
items.definition: In careful academic English, 'beg the question' means assuming what you are trying to prove; to mean 'prompt a question', say 'raise the question'.

items.sentence: Part of the reason most participants want a human in the loop is that someone must bear liability.
items.wrong: Part of the reason most participants want a human in the loop is because someone must bear liability.
items.right: Part of the reason most participants want a human in the loop is that someone must bear liability.
items.definition: After 'the reason is', use a that-clause; 'the reason is because' repeats the idea of reason and is avoided in formal writing.

Shadow the loop paragraph twice, then close it and summarise the post's answer in three sentences, one for possibility, one for impact and one for meaning.

loop.text: Software already runs much of the market, but running a market is a far cry from answering for it. Were many firms to rely on one model, their errors would tend to move in lockstep, and that model could become the system's Achilles' heel. Most participants in the IMF's outreach want a human in the loop, partly for reasons of liability; on our reading, accountability presupposes someone who can be asked why. A token counts as money only while a community keeps accepting it, so whether a machine-only token is money hinges on who does the accepting. What remains to be seen is whether machines could ever do it. Standard contracts cut both ways: they make checking easier, yet they can make firms more alike. A toy with ten banks is useful, with the caveat that it shows what could happen, not what will, so we should not read too much into it.
